DATE OF DISCHARGE:  10/06/2019



DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:  

1. Diverticulitis, refractory to medical treatment, diverticular abscess, not

amenable to percutaneous drainage due to small size and location behind the bladder

and surrounded by bowel. 

2. Postoperative bleeding requiring repeat laparoscopy without definitive finding of

bleeding site, although suspicious areas cauterized, hemostatic agents Allan

applied. 



HISTORY AND HOSPITAL COURSE:  A 50-year-old male patient admitted for abdominal

pain.  He has been treated for diverticulitis by Dr. Dilip Castanon with several

rounds of antibiotics since March.  He was referred to Dr. Fransisco Bergman for

urinary symptoms because he had pain on urination.  He was treated for 2 rounds of

antibiotics for prostatitis.  He continued to have pain, presented to the emergency

room, found to have a small 2.5 x 3 cm abscess behind the bladder surrounded by

bowel, not amenable due to a small size and location for percutaneous drainage.  The

patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics.  By the first 24 hours, he felt

better.  He then felt worse.  Decision was made for laparoscopic evaluation, which

he underwent on 10/03/2019 at about noon.  He had a small abscess, it was drained.

The sigmoid colon was plastered to the bladder and pelvic wall.  Attempted to take

this down, but it was too tightly adherent and it was felt that as the patient did

not want definitive colon resection at this time, it was hoped that drainage of his

abscess would relieve his symptoms and avoid a colon resection at this time.

Postoperatively, the patient initially did well in the recovery room with normal

blood pressure.  Initially, did well on transfer to the floor with normal blood

pressure.  He then began having acutely hypotensive later in the evening.  His

hemoglobin had dropped from 14 to 11.7 preoperatively and 9.7 postoperatively, and

because he was hypotensive and pale, he was taken to the operating room, where

laparoscopy revealed intra-abdominal blood that was evacuated.  He was given 1 unit

of blood normalizing his blood pressure.  The definitive bleeding site was not

found, although there were few areas that appeared possibly be suspicious and they

were cauterized.  Hemostatic agents were placed in the areas of initial dissection.

A drain was left in place.  Postoperatively, he did well.  His hemoglobin stabilized

and he was discharged home with a hemoglobin of 8.7.  He was sent home with

Augmentin for 10 days.  He is to follow up in my office in 1 week.  By the time of

discharge, he was feeling much better.  The preoperative pain resolved.  The patient

had a colonoscopy in the past with Dr. Mayorga five years ago, and at that time it was

told he had diverticulosis and a few polyps.  At this point, roze will see me in 1

week.  Continue oral antibiotics, and we will discuss the need for any future

surgical intervention based on his clinical course.

Name:  MARION LANZA

DISCHARGE DATE:  2019 
 
REASON FOR ADMISSION:  Abdominal pain. 
 
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:  Cardiopulmonary collapse due to multisystem organ failure secondary to sepsis as results of a bowel injury and intra-abdominal contamination. 
 
PROCEDURES PERFORMED:  She had a diagnostic laparoscopy with laparoscopic lysis of adhesions.  She also had an exploratory laparotomy and small bowel resection. 
 
HISTORY 
This patient is a 50-year-old who was referred to my office by Dr. Hill, a customer sales service manager in LifeCare Hospitals of North Carolina.  The patient was previously seen by Dr. Marcano in  for abdominal pain.  CT scan done in  showed focal abnormal segment of mid jejunum with wall thickening and ascites.  The patient had diffuse abdominal pain.  When she came to see me she already had an EGD and a colonoscopy done recently by Dr. Hill.  She had an MRCP done on 2019 that showed a prior cholecystectomy, but otherwise was negative.  She was in the ER on 2019 secondary to substernal chest pain.  She had a previous negative mesenteric arteriogram.  She came in to see me as a result of I \"did a good job\" as she said for her cousin Honey Dotson.  She has a past medical history of fibromyalgia and rheumatoid arthritis.  Dr. Hill as I said did an EGD and colonoscopy 3 months ago, which was normal.  She has an extensive past surgical history.  In , she had an exploratory laparotomy for abdominal pain where the gallbladder, appendix and one ovary were removed.  Dr. Escamilla of book retailer has done other surgery for abdominal pain and lysis of adhesions.  She later had an exploratory laparotomy and hysterectomy.  She reported having generalized abdominal pain, nausea, no appetite.  I discussed a diagnostic laparoscopy with lysis of adhesions.  I gave her a 50% chance this 
procedure would help and 50% chance she would feel no better.  She originally wanted to think about this and then called our office back to schedule.  The procedure was done on 11/19/2019, was about an hour worth of diagnostic laparoscopy with lysis of adhesions.  She had intra-abdominal adhesions seen throughout her abdomen.  We took these down with a combination of laparoscopic shelley and the 5 mm harmonic scalpel.  After surgery, she complained of abdominal pain and we admitted her to the hospital.  On postop day #1, I came in and saw her in the morniazucena.  She had tolerated liquids, voided and passed flatus, but had not ambulated.  She said she could not go home and asked if she could stay another day to walk and gain her strength back.  She was kept in the hospital.  The vital signs and things that day were fine in the morning when I saw her.  The vital signs at noon blood pressure 120/70 and heart rate of 87.  During the afternoon her urine output decreased and became very concentrated.  Our physician nurses assistant Dodie Amezquita was called.  She gave her a saline bolus 1 liter.  I was notified by the PA, I gave her a second bolus and then at 4:30 p.m. I was called by our PA to report that the heart rate was 140 and blood pressure of 85/52.  The abdomen was much more distended.  The PA had ordered a KUB.  I went down and found the patient in Radiology.  She looked like she was having significant abdominal pain and instead of ordering a CT scan or wasting time, I recommended she go directly to the operating room as I suspected there may be a bowel injury or other problem as she had deteriorated quite quickly over a 4-hour period of time.  It should be mentioned that her blood work the day after surgery was a white count 5.2, her hemoglobin was 12.9, hematocrit 42.2, platelet count of 320, her sodium was 141, potassium 3.8, chloride 106, bicarb was 28.  Glucose was elevated at 146, BUN was 17, creatinine was 0.89.  
Nothing appeared out of the ordinary on the board stacker hours of11/20.  She was taken to surgery.  She was found to be tachycardic and hypotensive.  She was found to have a bowel injury whether this was from a lysis of adhesions or a heat injury due to the harmonic scalpel was unsure, but it was placed in the small intestine.  There was contamination of the abdominal cavity.  There was exudate seen throughout and all of the intestines were tightly matted together.  I found the area where the perforation was, I was able to free up the bowel proximal and distal to this, I resected this area did a primary stapled anastomosis and then oversewed the opening in two 
layers where the staple had been in two layers.  She had a central line placed, nasogastric tube placed, Burke catheter placed and an arterial line placed.  She was brought to the intensive care unit in the Fall River General Hospital.  We did do a culture of the fluid and we washed her abdomen out with 5 meters of saline solution.  After surgery.  I consulted the hospitalist and the review specialist as well as infectious disease.  I saw her early the next morning at about 07:30.  She was still doing very poorly despite early intervention for her bowel injury.  She was tachycardic, on pressors and continued hypotension.  She was awake and able to follow commands. After obtaining the patient's informed consent, advising him of the risks

was identified and planned surgical sites were determined over the lumbar

incision as well as over the right gluteal region.  All regions were

anesthetized with 1% lidocaine with bicarb followed by 2% bupivacaine with

needles were inserted into the epidural space.  Inadvertent dural puncture

was obtained and a blood patch was performed simultaneously with the

procedure using 18 mL of autologous blood.  The leads were subsequently

placed without difficulty up to approximately the T8 region in a parallel

fashion.  Sixteen baton electrodes were utilized using a Continuum Rehabilitation system.  Trial with Airpersonsation was performed and good

stimulation was obtained in all affected necessary locations.  The

decision was made to continue with the implant.  Purse strings were placed

around each needle.  Distal stay sutures were placed.  The anchors had

already been placed over the electrodes.  The needles and sleeves were

removed and the anchors were secured with the existing 0 Mersilene ties.

generator.  Connectivity was satisfactory in 29 of the 32 electrodes.  The

decision was made to proceed with the implant.  All hex nuts were secured

irrigated with Betadine-containing irrigation solution.  Hemostasis was

inspected and was felt to be satisfactory in both surgical locations.  The

wounds were closed.  The pulse generator pocket was closed with a single

layer of 3-0 Polysorb using inverted vertical mattress sutures.  The skin

layers of 2-0 Vicryl.  The skin was then closed with beverly without

difficulty.  Sterile dressings were placed.  After completion of the

procedure, the patient was taken to the PACU for the postoperative care

and monitoring.

INDICATIONS FOR PROCEDURE:  This is a 39-year-old male, who in July of 2019

developed acute perforated diverticulitis requiring urgent surgery at

Bacharach Institute for Rehabilitatione facility and had a colectomy with Kaitlyn's procedure and

colostomy creation.  Surgery was complicated by midline wound infection

and dehiscence requiring prolonged localized wound care.  The patient had

recovered substantially since those events and was referred to me for

evaluation of colostomy takedown by his current primary care physician,

Dr. Tim Elliot.  The patient was seen in the office and noted to be

doing very well recovering, living a normal life with a colostomy,

comfortable, losing weight, being healthy, and without complication or

issues.  Given above and the six-month duration since acute events and

great recovery, colostomy takedown was indicated and recommended.  Risks,

benefits, alternatives were discussed with the patient in detail who

expressed understanding and consented to surgery.  Plan was for

laparoscopic assisted colostomy takedown, possible open.  Risks, benefits,

alternatives were discussed with the patient in detail.  Consent was

obtained.  The patient was scheduled for 12/16/2019.



OPERATIVE NOTE:  The patient was taken to the operating room and placed on

the operating table in lithotomy position with all bony prominences well

padded.  SCDs were placed.  Hernandez catheter was inserted using standard

sterile technique.  The patient was given 2 g of Ancef IV and 500 mg of

Flagyl IV one hour prior to cut time.  Preoperative time-out was taken to

identify the patient, procedure, operative staff, and surgical staff.

General anesthesia was induced and the patient was intubated.  The abdomen

was clipped, prepped, draped in standard surgical fashion.  The colostomy

was patched off using Ray-Brielle and Tegaderm.  An infraumbilical incision was

made using a fresh #15 scalpel and carried down to the fascia, which was

elevated and incised.  Entry into the abdomen was obtained using open

Blade technique.  A 12 mm Blade trocar was inserted and the abdomen was

insufflated to 12 to 15 mmHg.  The laparoscope was inserted and abdomen

was inspected.  No injury from initial trocar placement noted.  It was

clearly evident that there were extensive omental and bowel adhesions to

the anterior abdominal wall circumferentially, especially around the

midline.  A 5 mm trocar was placed at the inferior aspect of the prior

midline incision under direct visualization only few centimeters away from

the initial trocar placement.  Laparoscopic susan were used and gentle

dissection was had, but unfortunately it was clearly evident that there

was extensive adhesions and abdomen was somewhat hostile.  Therefore,

proceeding with laparoscopic colectomy would not be reasonable and

decision made to convert to open.  The trocars were removed and the

incision was carried utilizing the patient's prior midline abdominal

incision using a fresh #10 scalpel.  Incision was carried down to the

fascia with electrocautery and the abdomen was entered.  At this time, an

extensive open lysis of adhesions was performed freeing the omentum and

small bowel which were densely adhesed to the anterior abdominal wall.

Once this was completed, the colostomy was circumferentially dissected

out.  Following this, we turned our attention to the pelvis to see if we

can identify the rectal stump.  Approximately four strands of thick blue

Prolene sutures were identified in the pelvis, matted together with

adhesions of small bowel.  Slow gentle dissection was carried with

Metzenbaum scissors to dissect the small bowel out of the pelvis which was

deep into the pelvis and it was incarcerated and matted into the pelvis.

In doing so, it was also evident that the mid and tip of the appendix was

very densely adhesed within the pelvis as well along with the small bowel

and the remainder of these adhesions.  At this time, careful dissection

was carried through until all the bowel could be reduced from the pelvis

into the abdomen.  In doing so, one small enterotomy was made into the

small bowel and apex extending down into the pelvis.  This was repaired in

a two-layer fashion beginning with a 3-0 Vicryl running followed by 3-0

silk interrupted sutures.  Adequate repair without any significant loss of

bowel lumen was noted.  Hemostasis noted.  Furthermore, there was some

serosal tearing at the mid and distal appendix.  Given how the appendix

had significantly adhesed itself into the pelvis with the remainder of the

small bowel was going to be performed and the difficulty currently being

experienced during the surgery in the serosal tearing of the appendix,

decision was made to proceed with open appendectomy to ensure no

complication and adequately manage potential appendicitis, a very

difficult procedure and potential perforation of the appendix and the

distal of the appendix due to the inflammation, dissection necessary.  A

window was made between the appendix and the mesoappendix.  The

mesoappendix was divided using a linear JAMARCUS 55 mm stapler.  Following

this, the mesoappendix was divided using the Thunderbeat energy device.

Appendix sent off to pathology as specimen 1.  Following this, the small

bowel was significantly matted and also attached to the descending colon,

splenic flexure, as well as omentum, and on further dissection and

evaluation, it was evident that likely the patient had the white line of

Toldt on the left side mobilized prior given the amount of small bowel and

omental adhesions in the area.  Further extensive lysis adhesions carried

for the next hour to help for interloop and omental adhesions to be

dissected out carefully from the colon and to allow for proper

visualization of the anatomy.  Once this was completed, it was evident

there were some dense adhesions of the small bowel in the left upper

quadrant with proximal bowel being dilated and distal bowel being

compressed without a direct complete obstruction, but some signs of

potential partial obstruction or slowing of the bowel transit.  Once these

adhesions were resolved by the end of the procedure, the bowel was noted

to be significantly improved in such fashions.  Once the lysis of adhesion

was performed, the bowel was run from ligament of Treitz to the ileocecal

valve.  The small bowel was otherwise healthy without complication and no

other abnormalities other than a small enterotomy, which was repaired

during dissection out of the pelvis.  The mesoappendix was healthy and

viable.  The ascending colon, transverse colon that could be identified

were otherwise healthy and viable.  The stomach was otherwise healthy and

viable as well as the gallbladder and the liver.  There were some dense

adhesions of the left lobe of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall.

These were left alone.  Following this, small bowel was retracted toward

the right upper quadrant and care was taken to dissect out the colostomy.

Elliptical skin incision was made around the colostomy at the skin level

and was carried down through subcutaneous tissue down to the fascia, which

was divided.  The colostomy was brought into the abdomen and the area of

resection was identified and a window was made at the mesenteric edge and

a linear 55 mm stapler was used and the bowel was divided.  The mesentery

was divided using the Thunderbeat energy device.  The specimen was sent

off as colostomy/distal colectomy.  Following this, it was clearly evident

that there was not enough bowel length for proper anastomosis down into

the pelvis as there was already tension just at the same level and the

colostomy fascia level.  The white line of Toldt was redivided after

omental adhesions were taken down and there were significant omental

adhesions in the left upper quadrant around the splenic flexure as well.

The stomach was identified as well as transverse colon and the gastrocolic

ligament was divided and an omentectomy was performed to allow for better

visualization and clear identification of the anatomy and mobilization of

the splenic flexure.  Omentectomy was completed using the Thunderbeat

energy device.  Following this, the splenic flexure was mobilized to allow

for appropriate bowel length.  Once splenic flexure was mobilized, we were

able to clearly identify the distal descending colon that was remaining

following into the pelvis without tension to allow for primary anastomosis

that would be adequate and satisfactory.  Good viable distal bowel noted

with good blood supply.  Palpable arterial blood flow was clearly evident

at the distal aspect near the staple line.  Once this was all completed,

we turned our attention to the pelvis.  In the pelvis, there were a lot of

dense adhesions and inflammatory reaction as noted before as well as the

four strands of Prolene that were clearly evident.  These were believed to

be the lateral edges of the remaining distal colon.  In further dissecting

out, it was evident that a fair amount of the distal sigmoid colon was

left and the peritoneal reflection was approximately near 10 centimeters

distal to where the Prolene sutures were placed.  Given the patient's

history and these findings for appropriate reanastomosis, decision was

made to perform a distal sigmoid resection of the remaining portion of the

sigmoid colon to allow for proper colorectal anastomosis bypassing the

sigmoid colon that had prior significant diverticulitis and still has some

diverticula.  Of note, there was also some diverticula noted in the

ascending colon as it was examkirk during the procedure.  The remaining

sigmoid colon was circumferentially dissected out down to the peritoneal

reflection.  Once at the level of the peritoneal flexure in the proximal

rectum, the rectosigmoid colon was divided using TA-30 mm linear stapler.

The colon was cut and sent to pathology for review.  Good hemostasis was

noted from the staple line.  At this time, the abdomen was irrigated and

suctioned clear.  No bleeding was identified.  Good hemostasis noted.  The

bowel edges were viable and with good blood supply.  There was no tension

in the proposed anastomosis to be created.  No other issues or

complications noted.  The attention was turned to the prior colostomy site

fascia and a fairly large defect was clearly evident.  The fascia seen in

the abdominal wall defect was closed in a two-layer fashion beginning with

the anterior rectus sheath being reapproximated using a 0 Prolene running

suture followed by the posterior rectus sheath and peritoneum being

reapproximated using 0 Prolene running suture.  Following this, there was

clearly a large subcutaneous defect noted whi plans for repair at the

end of the procedure.  At this time, we turned our attention to performing

the primary end-to-end colorectal anastomosis.  The bowel edge was cut

from the distal end of the remaining distal colon and 20 mm EEA Anvil was

placed into the bowel lumen.  A 2-0 Prolene pursestring suture was then

placed and the Anvil appropriately fashioned without complication.  Good

hemostasis noted.  Following this, the 20 mm EEA stapler was entered

through the rectum after a rigid sigmoidoscopy was performed.  Of note, a

rigid sigmoidoscopy was performed at the beginning of the procedure as

well to ensure adequacy for continuing with the procedure as well as the

anoscopy which was performed in the office setting.  Some stool was

evacuated from the rectal vault and the EEA stapler was then entered into

the rectal vault and clearly identified and noted at the level of recently

placed rectal staple line.  The pin was deployed and brought through

without complication.  The Anvil and pin were attached and click was

identified and the staple line was closed.  The stapler was fired and then

removed.  The proximal and distal circular EEA stapler donuts were

evaluated on the nonsterile back table and clearly evident to be intact

without complication.  The Anvil and proximal circular staple line was

sent to pathology for review as proximal circular EEA staple line and the

distal circular staple line was sent to pathology for review as another

specimen as well.  At this time, decision made to proceed with a leak

test.  The bowel was grasped between two fingers proximally to the staple

line, and using the rigid sigmoidoscopy, the distal rectum was insufflated

with air.  Saline was placed into the pelvis and no leak was identified as

no bubbles were noted.  At this time, the pelvis was suctioned out and the

gas released from the rectum and the distal colon.  Appropriate

satisfactory end-to-end anastomosis was made without complication, without

leak, without tension and with good blood supply.  At this time, we

re-inspected the abdomen and no other issues or intraoperative

complications were noted.  The abdomen was hemostatic, the bowel in its

anatomical location, no tension and otherwise stable.  At this time, we

began the conclusion of our procedure.  The midline abdominal fascia was

reapproximated using a 0 running PDS loop suture.  Once this was

completed, the subcutaneous tissue was irrigated, cleansed, and hemostasis

obtained using electrocautery.  There was a large defect in the prior

colostomy site given the patient's size and habitus and it was fairly deep

subcutaneous tissue.  Plans were for primary closure in the patient's best

interest about having a large wound and therefore adjacent tissue transfer

with skin and subcutaneous flap were decided for the closure so that the

defect can be closed after the area was suctioned and cleaned.  The

patient had a large wound that required prolonged care.  The subcutaneous

tissue was elevated off the fascia from the midline laterally towards the

prior colostomy defect.  Once reached, it was circumferentially dissected

around this level as well and further laterally superior and inferiorly.

Once this was completed, the skin was reapproximated using surgical skin

alan followed by reapproximation of the mobilized subcutaneous tissue

beneath the dermis using 3-0 Vicryl sutures.  The remaining tissue was

then allowed to freely extend over the remaining of the fascia, which was

released from without any defects.  Good hemostasis noted.  Appropriate

positioning noted without any remaining defects.  The right-sided fascia

and subcutaneous tissue were elevated and released to allow for

mobilization medially as well to allow for less tension.  The skin

incision was then reapproximated using surgical skin alan.  Dressings

were then applied.  The patient tolerated the procedure well, was

extubated, taken to postanesthetic care unit in stable condition.

draped and prepped in the usual sterile fashion in dorsal lithotomy position.

abdomen where a Veress needle was used at the umbilicus.  The abdomen was

insufflated with CO2 gas to approximately 3.5 liters.  An 8 mm infraumbilical

incision was made.  The trocar as well as the laparoscope was inserted under

direct visualization then two 8 mm left lateral ports were placed for robotic 
arm

two and the assist port, and on the right an 8 mm port placed for robotic arm

one.  The patient was placed in Trendelenburg.  Dense bowel and bladder 
adhesions

noted.  At this point the bladder and the uterus was found to be fixed 
anteriorly. The manipulator appeared to be in the potential space between the

bladder and the uterus.  The uterine manipulator appeared not to be in the 
uterus

at this point.  Given that the Baer catheter was clear with urine, no evidence

of any other trauma noted, we decided to proceed.  The robot was brought to the

patient's right side and the camera port was docked in the usual fashion.  The

targeting was performed and the two remaining arms were then docked.  A vessel 
sealer was placed in arm one and bipolar grasper in arm two.  I then unscrubbed

and went to the surgeon console to begin the surgery.

 

At this point, using the bipolar grasper and the vessel sealer, the adhesions on

the left side were freed up all the way down to the infundibulopelvic ligament.

At this point, the infundibulopelvic ligament was cauterized and cut using the

vessel sealer.  This was taken down to include the round ligament all the way

down to the uterine artery.  The opposite side was done on a similar fashion.

after taking both infundibulopelvic ligaments all the way down to the uterine

arteries, I then carefully dissected the uterus off the peritoneum of the

bladder.  There was no abdominal injury noted to the bladder at this point.  The

bladder was retrograde filled with normal saline.  Again, no extravasation of

fluid in the abdomen, however, some leakage was noted through the vagina after

removal of the manipulator.  Anterior colpotomy and posterior colpotomy was

performed.  The uterus, cervix, tubes and ovaries were removed through the

vagina.  The vaginal cuff closed robotically using #2-0 V-Loc suture in a 
running

fashion.  The peritoneum over the bladder was also closed using the #2-0 V-Loc

suture.  Pelvis copiously irrigated with normal saline.  Both ureters were

visualized, no evidence of any injury.  The ovaries were removed with the 
uterus.

injured, I then unscrubbed.  One 1 mL of Furocin  was given by the

anesthesiologist to help with the cystoscopy.  The inadvertant vaginal cystotomy

days

and will follow the patProMedica Toledo Hospital as an outpatient for bladder cystogram.  I will

with the patient in recovery and prior to discharge.  Dr. Donald will dictate

drainage.  I then turned my attention to the abdomen where the robotic trocars

were removed and the laparoscopic ports were closed using #3-0 Vicryl in a

subcuticular fashion.  0.25% Marcaine placed for postoperative pain.

room in stable condition.

numbness, and improved overall mobility and function. 

Alternatives include no surgery.  All questions were answered. 

The patient and his family understood and agreed to the procedure. 

Informed consent was obtained, witnessed, and verified. The patient's lumbar 
spine was marked, and he was then assessed by the anesthesia and nursing teams.
  He then received an erector spinae/TLIP block in the pre-operative holding 
area.  The patient was then taken to the operating room. 

  

Procedure:

The patient was brought into the operating room, where general anesthesia was 
administered.  

This included 2g IV Ancef, 1g IV Vancomycin, and 1g IV tranexamic acid (TXA).

A time-out was done led by yennifer, the attending surgeon.

An indwelling Cramer catheter was successfully inserted by the nursing team.

The intra-operative neuromonitoring team provided prepositioning baseline motor 
and sensory readings. 

The patient was then safely placed in a prone position with all bony 
prominences well-padded on a Hugh Chatham Memorial Hospitalo OSI spine table with strict attention paid 
to maintenance of sagittal vertical alignment. Retroversion of the pelvis was 
avoided by ensuring that the hips were extended. This also ensured appropriate 
lumbar lordosis. The arms were placed on well-padded arm boards and maintained 
with standard forward flexion, abduction, and external rotation of the shoulders
, and flexion of the elbows.  

Special attention was given to the safe positioning of the cervical spine.

The patients eyes and belly were all free. The table was placed in 7 degrees 
of reverse Trendelenburg position. 

Post-positional motor and sensory readings confirmed no change.

A C-arm fluoroscopy unit was positioned perpendicularly to the table and 
maintained at the level of the upper thoracic spine, except when needed.

The skin was prepped in standard, sterile fashion using betadine prep & scrub, 
wiped off with alcohol, and DuraPrep applied. Standard window draping was 
utilized, and this included draping of the C-arm.

Appropriate pre-operative imaging, including lumbar spine x-rays and MRI, were 
available throughout the case for intraoperative evaluation. Verification of 
the intended surgical levels was confirmed with a lateral fluoroscopic x-ray 
using a Peter elevator for localization.

A time-out was repeated, and the case began.



A midline skin incision was performed from the tip of the spinous process of L1 
to the tip of the spinous process of S1.  

Using electrocautery, the dissection was carried down through subcutaneous fat 
and then through the midline of the lumbodorsal fascia down to the tips of the 
spinous processes.  A subperiosteal dissection was performed using a 
combination of unipolar electrocautery and Peter elevation. This was carried 
down the spinous process, over the laminae, across the facet joints, and out 
over the tips of the transverse processes from L2 to L5.  In this dissection, 
the capsule of the L1-L2 and L5-S1 joints were preserved bilaterally.  The L2-L3
, L3-L4, and L4-L5 joint capsules were resected using a combination of 
electrocautery and mechanical resection with rongeurs.  The posterolateral 
dissection was performed with attention to hemostatis by utilizing both 
unipolar as well as bipolar electrocautery. The posterolateral/inter-transverse 
space was packed with Ray-Emil sponges.  

A Kocher clamp was placed over an arbitrary interspinous space of the lower 
lumbar spine and, once again, a lateral fluoroscopic x-ray helped identify the 
correct levels for dissection.



On MRI, the theca was noted to be stenosed, particularly at L3-L4, and L4-L5 
with a spondylolisthesis at L3-L4. At L2-L3, and L4-L5, considerable facet 
joint hypertrophy was contributing to lateral recess stenosis.

The entirety of the L2, L3, and L4 laminae was resected utilizing Kerrison 
rongeur upcuts combined with Leksell rongeurs.  Bilateral and central 
laminotomies were performed at the cephalad end of the lamina of L5. All 
harvested bone was saved, freed of fibrous tissue, and milled with a bone mill.

An angled ball-tipped feeler was utilized to demonstrate stenosis of the 
lateral recesses and neuroforaminae of L2-L3, L3-L4, and L4-L5.

Next, an osteotome was utilized to longitudinally split the pars 
interarticularis and the inferior facet of L2, L3, and L4 bilaterally. The 
osteotomized bone was imploded towards the thecal sac, which was protected with 
cottonoid patties, and removed with either a Leksell rongeur or a Kerrison 
ronguer.

Upon removal of all osteotomized bone, we gained clear and easy access to the 
superior facets of L3, L4, and L5, where tight recess stenosis was again 
appreciated.

The exiting L2, L3, and L4 nerve roots were identified and protected.

The medial aspect of the superior facets was resected at each level bilaterally 
using Kerrison rongeurs. Enough superior facet was resected to guarantee a 
patent neural foramen at ech level. This required excess of 50% total facet 
resection at L2-L3, L3-L4, and L4-L5. This freed the theca and the exiting 
nerve roots at each level.

Again, the foraminae bilaterally at L2-L3, L3-L4, and L4-L5 were inspected 
utilizing an angled ball-tipped probe and proved to be generously capacious in 
accommodating the unobstructed exit of the nerve root at that level.

The crowding of the convoluted ligamentum flavum and posterior facet joint 
capsules also contributed to the recess stenosis. These structures were excised 
using Kerrison upcuts, thus fully completing the decompression.  



All retractors were relaxed and removed.

A Jamshidi needle was delivered into the left posterior ileum throAurora St. Luke's Medical Center– Milwaukee the same 
surgical incision. Via this, 60 mL of bone marrow was aspirated and spun down 
to isolate a mix of osteoprogenitor and hematopoietic cells.



Retractors were inserted once again.

The following was performed at L2-L3, L3-L4, and also at L4-L5:

The theca was gently mobilized from right to left using a nerve root retractor.
  In order to do this, we ensured that each nerve root was completely free in 
its neural foramen as previously described.

With the disc clearly visualized, large epidural veins were cauterized using 
bipolar electrocaumarcelino. The disc was approached from the right side and using a 
#11-blade, an elliptical annulotomy was performed. Gabriela were passed into the 
disc at each level.  At each level the discs were morselized with rotation of 
the gabriela, and then extricated with pituitary rongeurs and saved for lab 
evaluation.  The end plates were freed of all soft tissues using a serrated 
curette.

Milled bone autograft was packed into the interbody space, thus completing an 
anterior arthrodesis of the intervertebral space.

At L2-L3, a size 11mm x 22mm Fortilink Tetrafuse spacer was inserted. 

At L3-L4, a size 13mm x 22mm Fortilink Tetrafuse spacer was inserted. 

At L4-L5, a size 13mm x 22mm Fortilink Tetrafuse spacer was inserted. 

Each spacer was packed with bone autograft prior to insertion.



The cages were placed in a Press-Fit type manner where the gabriela were one 
size under the actual size of the spacer used as outlined above.

An interference fit of the cage assured as we relied on ligamentotaxis for 
fixation.

The address the axial segmental instability of each level, due to loss of disc 
height, that further contributed to neuroforaminal stenosis.

Reconstitution of disc height was achieved. 

The L4-L5 level was addressed first, followed by the L3-L4 level, and then 
followed by the L2-L3 level.



The thecal sac was adherent and stuck down to the right lateral wall of the 
bony vertebral canal.  While freeing this adherent dura, a durotomy occurred in 
the axilla of the right L2 nerve root. A successful primary dural repair was 
performed using 4-0 Nurolon suture.  The success of the repair was confirmed 
with 2 separate Valsalva maneuvers, up to 35mmHg, sequentially performed.

No other dural problems were encountered, and the thecal sac otherwise appeared 
healthy throughout the procedure. 



Pedicle screws were then seated bilaterally from L2-L5 utilizing standard 
anatomical guidelines: IE the intersection of the horizontal axis of the 
transverse process with the longitudinal axis of the inferior facet at each 
level.  

Utilizing lateral fluoroscopic x-ray, a 4.5mm pneumatic drill was passed via 
the pedicle at each level, into the corresponding vertebral body. Imaging 
allowed us to ensure that the drill screw was delivered along the undersurface 
of each endplate.  This was the best quality bone in this bone bed.  

Each pedicle was palpated with a ball tip feeler.  No breech of anterior, medial
, lateral, caudal or cranial bone bed was noted.  

Size 6.5x40mm Precision screws were inserted from L2 to L5.  

Each screw was reevaluated with lateral and anteroposterior fluoroscopy as well 
as intraoperative neuromonitoring.  

All intraoperative neuromonitoring readings were at or above the safe passage 
of 10 mA.

The L2, L3, L4, and L5 pedicles were inspected and palpated using an angled ball
-tipped probe. There was no evidence of screw breach involving any of the 
pedicles.



Next, two rods were inserted and fixed into the screw heads with the 
appropriate screw caps.  A torque-limiting device completed the fixation of 
each cap into each screw head. 

A crosslink was utilized to add rotational stability to the construct.



The muscle was gently retracted off the intertransverse plane.  All packing 
sponges were removed.

Milled autologous bone, with allograft expansion, was combined with the bone 
marrow aspirate concentrate and used for the posterolateral arthrodesis along 
the intertransverse plane from L2 to L5.  The recipient bone bed was denuded of 
all soft tissue.  No burring was necessary due to healthy bleeding of each bony 
surface, including the posterior surface of the transverse processes and the 
lateral surface of the pars interarticularis at each level. 



Throughout the case, the wound was irrigated with normal saline solution to 
keep the exposed soft tissues hydrated. The retractors were released every 15 
to 20 minutes to enable adequate blood flow to the paraspinal muscles. These 
muscles were gently massaged upon release of the retractors to further 
facilitate blood flow.

At the end of the procedure, fragmented and compromised paraspinal muscle was 
superficially debrided.

The dura was inspected and was watertight and completely intact.

The durotomy repair was covered with 3 layers of Surgicel and then encased in 
DuraSeal.



Closure:

The paraspinal muscles and overlying lumbodorsal fascia were closed in the 
midline using #1 vicryl sutures in simple interrupted fashion. 

A  HemDomingo hansonain was placed in the plane superficial to the fascia, exiting 
adjacent to the proximal apex of the incision.  The drain cannister was 
maintained on gravity suction with no negative pressure self-suction applied.

The wound was repeatedly thoroughly irrigated with normal saline solution.

The subcutaneous tissues were closed using #1 vicryl sutures.

The skin was closed using a running 2-0 Biosyn absorbable suture.

This completed a complex, 4-layered wound closure of approximately 20cm. 

The skin was then painted with benzoin and Steri-Strips were applied 
perpendicular to the incision.

A Primapore adhesive Telfa island dressing was applied over the Steri-Strips 
and a sterile, compressive dressing was applied using 4x4 gauze pads.

The skin was painted with DuraPrep.

The wound was then sealed with adhesive Ioban.



Final AP & lateral fluoroscopic analysis revealed L2-L3, L3-L4, and L4-L5 PLIF 
cages and L2-L5 instrumentation that appeared intact & place.

The L2-L3, L3-L4, and L4-L5 disc heights were reconstituted with visibly patent 
neuroforaminae.

There was no fluoroscopic evidence of retained sponges or needles.

The sponge and needle counts were correct at the end of the case and I, the 
attending surgeon, was present and scrubbed throughout the case.

The patient was transferred to a hospital bed. All neural monitoring leads were 
removed.

The patient was then transferred to the recovery room in stable condition, as 
per the anesthesia team, having tolerated the procedure well.



Overall comment:  All appropriate goals were achieved in the execution of this 
operative event.  Patient to be nursed initially in the ICU.

OPERATIVE INDICATIONS: This is a 20-year-old female who was brought to the

operating room by Dr. Muñoz for removal of what appeared to be a Rena's

duct cyst. During the procedure there was an inadvertent cystotomy. During her

closure of the cystotomy the trigone of the bladder appeared to be more puckered
up

than normal and there was concern about potential obstruction to the left

ureter due to this. I was called to the operating room to evaluate and help.



DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE: At the time I came in the patient was already prepped

and draped in dorsal lithotomy position. The closure of the bladder had been

performed. Of note, the bladder closure appeared to be watertight. Rigid

cystoscopy was performed. There was a moderate amount of blood clots at the

base of the bladder. A Urovac was then utilized to evacuate the clots from the 
bladder.

A  Bugbee was utilized to cauterize some bleeding vessels at the middle

of the trigone. Once done I examined the bladder and the trigone did appear a 
little bit abnormal 

due to the closure. With that said, both ureteral orifices did appear to efflux 
clear

urine. At this point a 5-Citizen of Seychelles open-ended ureteral catheter was utilized to

obtain a retrograde pyelogram on the right side first. There was no 
extravasation.

There were no filling defects and there was no hydronephrosis. Next a retrograde

pyelogram was performed on the left side. Similarly, there was no

extravasation, filling defects, or hydronephrosis. Given the closure was on the

left side of the bladder and there was concern about still possible obstruction

to the left ureter. I therefore decided to place a stent on that side. A 
guidewire was

advanced up the left collecting system and the 5-Citizen of Seychelles open-ended ureteral

catheter was removed. The guidewire was utilized to advance a 7-Citizen of Seychelles x 22-32 
cm

JJ ureteral stent up into the left collecting system. Of note, there did appear

to be a little bit more resistance than normal while advancing the stent up the

left collecting system. With that said, I was also able to get the

proximal end extended into the left kidney. The guidewire was then removed and

there were adequate curls of the stent in the left renal pelvis and in the

bladder.



I then confirmed good hemostasis inside the bladder and then removed the 
cystoscope.

An 18-Citizen of Seychelles Anderson catheter was inserted into the bladder. The balloon was 
filled

with 10 mL of sterile water and the catheter was connected to gravity drainage.

This marked the conclusion of the procedure. The patient was taken out of

dorsal lithotomy position, awakened from anesthesia and transferred to the

recovery room in stable condition.



ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS: 10 mL.



COMPLICATIONS: None.



SPECIMEN: None.



PLAN: I will keep the patient's catheter in for 2 weeks. Her stent will be kept

in for at least 2 weeks as well. I will arrange follow up in urology office for

both catheter and stent removal. A cystogram will be done prior to removal of 
the

catheter.

BRIEF HISTORY AND INDICATIONS:

The patient is a very pleasant 76-year-old male, who presented to the Herington Municipal Hospital Emergency Department on 09/17/2019 with moderate axial low back pain and

severe right lower extremity pain.  Additional associated symptoms and

complaints included progressive motor and sensory deficits in both of his lower

extremities, right greater than left to the degree that he was having trouble

with ambulation.  An MRI of the patient's lumbar spine obtained at the time of

admission demonstrated severe osseous and soft tissue spinal stenosis at the

L2-L3 level with a very large right paracentral herniated nucleus pulposus with

an extruded fragment together, which was creating severe compression on the

nerve roots and thecal sac at L2-L3 level.  On exam, the patient had motor and

sensory deficits in both the L2 and L3 dermatomal distributions of the right

lower extremity.  Given the patient's clinical history, level of disability in

the presence of a progressive neurologic deficit, surgical decompression of the

patient's lumbar spine was recommended.  Surgical treatment was delayed

secondary to the patient being on Plavix.  It was recommended that surgical

decompression of the neural elements of the spine was delayed until the patient

could be off Plavix for several days so as to prevent the potential

catastrophic-associated complication of epidural hematoma.  The patient

discussed the risks and benefits of holding his Plavix with both the hospitalist

and his velvet steamer.  The patient agreed to accept the risk of holding his

Plavix and agreed to proceed as recommended.  I discussed the recommended

surgical treatment with the patient in detail including the risks, benefits,

potential complications, expected outcomes, indications and alternatives.  Those

risks that were discussed included, but were not limited to significant and

possibly life-threatening bleeding, infection, spinal fluid leaks, paralysis,

potential damage to surrounding neurovascular and soft tissue structures,

iatrogenic instability, potential serious reactions to anesthesia, and potential

need for secondary surgical procedures.  The patient gave informed written

consent to proceed as planned after all of his questions were addressed and

answered to his satisfaction.



PROCEDURE NOTE:

After correctly identifying the patient in the preoperative holding area and

after his operative site was appropriately marked, he was transferred to the

operating room.  Once in the operating room, he had successful induction of

general endotracheal anesthesia, then he was transferred to a radiolucent

Kris OR table and placed in the prone position.  All bony prominences were

meticulously padded.  Bilateral upper extremities were placed in the safe

position.  The operative site was then prepped and draped in the routine sterile

fashion.  Prior to beginning the case, we completed an operating room timeout

with all parties involved in the case and agreement and verified appropriate

infusion of prophylactic antibiotics.



Using an 18-gauge spinal needle in the paraspinal soft tissues and lateral C-arm

image, the L2-L3 spinal level was localized and marked on the skin with a

sterile marking pen.  After infusion of local anesthetic, a 10 blade scalpel was

used to incise the skin and subcutaneous tissue.  Bovie cautery and Allen

elevator were then used to perform bilateral paraspinal subperiosteal

dissection, exposing the posterior elements at the L2-L3 level.  A #4 Penfield

elevator was placed in L2-L3 interlaminar space and then lateral C-arm image

confirmed that indeed L2-L3 spinal level had been localized and exposed.  L2-L3

laminectomy/medial facetectomies was then performed with use of Leksell rongeur,

high-speed bur, and a series of Kerrison rongeurs and curettes.  Once

laminectomy was performed, we did encounter a very large right paracentral

herniated nucleus pulposus with a large extruded fragment, which was creating a

severe compression of the neural elements at L2-L3 level.  This herniated

nucleus pulposus and extruded fragment was removed in its entirety carefully

with a series of curettes and pituitary rongeurs.  During the decompression of

the lateral recess on the right side, an incidental durotomy was created.  This

durotomy was repaired quite successfujoe with a running 6-0 Nurolon stitch. 

Adequate decompression of all of the neural elements was then confirmed with use

of Marisela elevator and nerve hook.  We supplemented our durotomy repair with

Duragen sponge and Tisseel dural sealant.  Once decompression and durotomy

repair were complete, Valsalva maneuver performed per anesthesia

intraoperatively confirmed that there were no persistent spinal fluid leaks

prior to closure.  Medium Hemovac drain was then placed deep to the fascia and

placed on gravity suction only.  The wound was then closed in layers in standard

fashion using Stratafix suture for the deep fascia, 2-0 Vicryl for the

subcutaneous tissue, and a running 4-0 Monocryl subcuticular stitch and

Dermabond glue for the skin.  The patient has sterile dressing applied followed

by being awakened and extubated in the operating room without incident.  He was

then transferred to the PACU in stable condition and he tolerated the procedure

quite well without complications.  All counts were correct at the end of the

case.

BRIEF HISTORY:

The patient is a 35-year-old lady with a longstanding history of menorrhagia

secondary to symptomatic fibroids, which had led to iron-deficiency anemia

requiring blood transfusions.  She continued to bleed despite Lupron injections

and after discussing management options with the patient, she opted to proceed

with hysterectomy with removal of her tubes. The patient understands that a

hysterectomy will render her sterile. She is a mother of 5 children, the last

childbirth was 10 years ago, and she is adamant that her family is complete.

Risks and alternatives to surgery were discussed extensively with her including

but not limited to bleeding, infection, injury to bowel, ureter, bladder, blood 
vessels,

and other vital organs, the risk of thromboembolic events and also

the risk of anesthesia.  She consented to proceed with the surgery. Her preop

hemoglobin 2 weeks prior to surgery was 7.4 g/dL and she was transfused 3 units 
of

packed red blood cells a week prior to the planned procedure with a resultant 
hemoglobin

of 12 g/dL.

 

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE:

The patient was taken to the operating room, where induction of general

anesthesia was performed without difficulty. She was placed in dorsal lithotomy

position after adequate level of anesthesia. The abdomen, perineum, and vagina

were prepped in the usual sterile fashion for laparoscopic vaginal surgery.  A

Gaona catheter was placed and backfilled with 30 mL of dilute methylene blue

dye.  She received 1 g of Ancef and SCDs were in place. Appropriate time-

out was held. A bimanual examination revealed a mobile uterus approximately 10

weeks' size.  A open side bivalve speculum was then placed into the vagina and 
the

anterior lip of the cervix was grasped with an Allis clamp.  The uterus was

sounded and a Be-Bound uterine manipulator was placed into the cavity to aid

uterine manipulation.  The instruments and the Allis clamp were then removed.

marketing communication manager's glove was changed.  The attention was turned to the abdomen, where

the infraumbilical area was infiltrated with 0.25% of Marcaine.  A 5 mm incision

was made with a scalpel.  Tenting the anterior abdominal wall upwards, a Veress

needle was introduced into the abdominal cavity with an opening pressure of 5

mmHg noted.  CO2 insufflation was performed and an adequate pneumoperitoneum of

13 mmHg was achieved.  A 5 mm port was then placed through this incision and

correct placement was confirmed with the laparoscope.  Two additional incisions

were placed under direct visualization, 2 cm medial and cephalad from the

anterior superior iliac spine on both the right and the left side.  The uterus

was lifted and elevated out of the pelvis and inspected with the aforementioned

findings noted.  The ureters were identified on either sides.  Starting from the

left side, the left fallopian tube was grasped with an atraumatic grasper and

the routine salpingectomy was performed ligating and cutting along the 

mesosalpinx using a 5 mm ligature device until the cornua of the uterus was 
reached. 

The round ligament was then grasped and ligated and cut and the anterior lip of 
the broad

ligament was incised and a bladder flap was created. The posterior lip of the 
broad ligament 

was also incised exposed the the uterine vessels. Once the vessels were 
skeletonized 

adequately, the vessels were then double ligated and cut. 

This process was repeated on the right side and the bladder flap was

completed anteriorly. Once this was completed, the abdomen was desufflated and

all the instruments were removed from the abdomen. Attention was then turned to

the vagina to complete the surgery. A weighted speculum was placed into the

vagina posteriorly. The bladder was released. Using lateral wall retractors,

tenaculum were then used to grasp the cervix anteriorly and posteriorly.  The

cervix was then circumscribed using electrocautery. The vaginal mucosa was

pushed away anteriorly and posteriorly. The posterior cul-de-sac was then

entered sharply performing the colpotomy and the weighted speculum was exchanged

for a Gonzalez-Auvard speculum which was placed into the peritoneal cavity.

Anterior colpotomy was performed easily by sharp dissection, making sure that

the finger was palpated along the dissection that had been made

laparoscopically.  A right angle retractor was then placed anteriorly pushing

the bladder cephalad.  The uterosacral ligaments on both sides were crossclamped

with a Jose clamp, cut, and ligated using Jose suture of 2-0 Polysorb.

inspecting the right side, an intra-op consultation was called to the urologist,

of the

sutures on the right side. This was done under direct visualization

laparoscopically and the vaginal cuff was re-opened from the right side to the

midline and the sutures on the right side were taken down.  The urologist had

arrived at this junction and advised that we should go ahead and repeat the

cystoscopy.  The cystoscopy was repeated, but still there was no efflux of urine

from the right side.  He then took over the procedure and went ahead to perform

a cystoscopy and other procedures  to ascertain patency of the right

ureter.  The patency of the right ureter was not established with various

procedures by the urologist.  At this juncture, a decision was made to go ahead

and perform an exploratory laparotomy with the aim of identifying the ureter and

performing the necessary repair.  I then re-closed the vaginal cuff with 0

patient's vagina.  The laparoscopic skin incisions were closed with subcuticular

  Dehydration, Pediatric  Dehydration occurs when your child loses more fluids from the body than he or she takes in. Vital organs such as the kidneys, brain, and heart cannot function without a proper amount of fluids. Any loss of fluids from the body can cause dehydration.   Children are at a higher risk of dehydration than adults. Children become dehydrated more quickly than adults because their bodies are smaller and use fluids as much as 3 times faster.   CAUSES   · Vomiting.    · Diarrhea.    · Excessive sweating.    · Excessive urine output.    · Fever.    · A medical condition that makes it difficult to drink or for liquids to be absorbed.  SYMPTOMS   Mild dehydration  · Thirst.  · Dry lips.  · Slightly dry mouth.  Moderate dehydration  · Very dry mouth.  · Sunken eyes.  · Sunken soft spot of the head in younger children.  · Dark urine and decreased urine production.  · Decreased tear production.  · Little energy (listlessness).  · Headache.  Severe dehydration  · Extreme thirst.    · Cold hands and feet.  · Blotchy (mottled) or bluish discoloration of the hands, lower legs, and feet.  · Not able to sweat in spite of heat.  · Rapid breathing or pulse.  · Confusion.  · Feeling dizzy or feeling off-balance when standing.  · Extreme fussiness or sleepiness (lethargy).    · Difficulty being awakened.    · Minimal urine production.    · No tears.  DIAGNOSIS   Your health care provider will diagnose dehydration based on your child's symptoms and physical exam. Blood and urine tests will help confirm the diagnosis. The diagnostic evaluation will help your health care provider decide how dehydrated your child is and the best course of treatment.   TREATMENT   Treatment of mild or moderate dehydration can often be done at home by increasing the amount of fluids that your child drinks. Because essential nutrients are lost through dehydration, your child may be given an oral rehydration solution instead of water. 
  Severe dehydration needs to be treated at the hospital, where your child will likely be given intravenous (IV) fluids that contain water and electrolytes.   HOME CARE INSTRUCTIONS  · Follow rehydration instructions if they were given.    · Your child should drink enough fluids to keep urine clear or pale yellow.    · Avoid giving your child:  · Foods or drinks high in sugar.  · Carbonated drinks.  · Juice.  · Drinks with caffeine.  · Fatty, greasy foods.  · Only give svcd-rue-bnnhlbd or prescription medicines as directed by your health care provider. Do not give aspirin to children.    · Jesúsep all follow-up appointments.  SEEK MEDICAL CARE IF:  · Your child's symptoms of moderate dehydration do not go away in 24 hours.  · Your child who is older than 3 months has a fever and symptoms that last more than 2-3 days. Inc.    Pneumonia, Child  Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs.   CAUSES   Pneumonia may be caused by bacteria or a virus. Usually, these infections are caused by breathing infectious particles into the lungs (respiratory tract).  Most cases of pneumonia are reported during the fall, winter, and early spring when children are mostly indoors and in close contact with others. The risk of catching pneumonia is not affected by how warmly a child is dressed or the temperature.  SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS   Symptoms depend on the age of the child and the cause of the pneumonia. Common symptoms are:  · Cough.  · Fever.  · Chills.  · Chest pain.  · Abdominal pain.  · Feeling worn out when doing usual activities (fatigue).  · Loss of hunger (appetite).  · Lack of interest in play.  · Fast, shallow breathing.  · Shortness of breath.  A cough may continue for several weeks even after the child feels better. This is the normal way the body clears out the infection.  DIAGNOSIS   Pneumonia may be diagnosed by a physical exam. A chest X-ray examination may be done. Other tests of your child's blood, urine, or sputum may be done to find the specific cause of the pneumonia.  TREATMENT   Pneumonia that is caused by bacteria is treated with antibiotic medicine. Antibiotics do not treat viral infections. Most cases of pneumonia can be treated at home with medicine and rest. More severe cases need hospital treatment.  HOME CARE INSTRUCTIONS   · Cough suppressants may be used as directed by your child's health care provider. Keep in mind that coughing helps clear mucus and infection out of the respiratory tract. It is best to only use cough suppressants to allow your child to rest. Cough suppressants are not recommended for children younger than 5 years old. For children between the age of 5 years and 5 years old, use cough suppressants only as directed by your child's health care provider.  · If your child's health care provider prescribed an 
antibiotic, be sure to give the medicine as directed until it is all gone.  · Give medicines only as directed by your child's health care provider. Change the water daily.  · Offer your child fluids to loosen the mucus.  · Be sure your child gets rest. Coughing is often worse at night. BP remained stable in CT where he was noted to have a grade V splenic laceration and a left sided pneumothorax. He was emergently transferred to the OR for Laparotomy    PROCEDURE:  The patient was escorted to the operating room by anesthesia and placed supine on the OR table. Pre-op abx were give, SCDs were placed and he underwent induction of general anesthesia. He had previously been intubated in the trauma bay and nunez and OGT had already been inserted. A timeout was called to identify the correct patient and procedure.   The abdomen was prepped and draped in sterile fashion. An upper midline laparotomy incision was made with the 10 blade scalpel and carried down to the fascia sharply. The fascia was scored with the cautery, lifted with vitaly clamps and the peritoneum was sharply entered. The remainder of the fascia was opened with cautery.  Once the abomen was entered there was a large volume hemoperitoneum that was suctioned. The left upper quadrant was packed with laparotomy pads and clot was removed. A Cruz retractor was inserted and the abdominal wall retracted to visualize the spleen which appeared shattered 
andlateral attachments had already been autodissected by hematoma. Clots were evacuated and the spleen was medialized by bluntly taking down any remaining attachments to the colon and lateral abdominal wall. Most of the gastrosplenic ligament was already avulsed from the spleen. The hilum was identified and a Malian clamp was placed across. The hilum was transected with curved solitario scissors. The spleen was removed and sent to pathology. All vascular pedicles were ligated with 0-silk suture. Bleeding points were cauterized. Packs were replaced in the left upper quadrant and slowly removed to identify any further bleeding. In order to identify the splenic vessels more carefully, the gastrocolic ligament was opened with the Enseal device and the lesser sac was entered. There was some clot coming from the lesser sac. The pancreas was identified posterior to the stomach and appeared intact with mild contusion. The splenic vessels were unable to be safely identified here due to the patients body habitus and large amount of visceral adipose. We were then able to trace back the splenic vessels from the cut hilum, dissect around them and place an 0-silk suture ligature.. The abdomen was copiously irrigated to remove all remaining old blood and clots. All four quadrants were inspected for any further signs of bleeding. There was still a large volume of hemoperitoneum in the right upper quadrant that was evacuated. The liver was palpated, no injury was identified. The gallbladder and hepatic flexure and colon mesentery appeared intact. The right and left lower quadrants as well ans the pelvis were also inspected. Remaining blood and clots were evacuated and no continued bleeding was noted. There did not appear to be any other injuries. We irrigated the abdomen once more. Once satisfied with hemostasis, the midline fascia of the incision was closed with running 0-looped PDS x2. The wound was irrigated and skin was closed with 
margy and covered with sterile dressings.     A left sided chest tube was then inserted. An incision was made at the 4th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line with a 10 blade.subcutaneous tissues were dissected with a tonsil and the pleural cavity was bluntly entered. The lung was palpated and swept away form the thoracic cavity. A 32 Fr chest tube was inserted and secured with an 0-silk suture. The chest tube was connected to an atrium and placed on suction. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was sent to SICU in critical condition, Butler Memorial Hospitalng intubated. Sponge counts were not able to be made correctly, thus an intra-operative xray was performed which did not identify any retained foreign body. Dr. Kirksey was present and scrubbed for the entire case.     Electronically signed by Martine Prado MD on 9/15/19 at 10:50 AM

Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters and Midline Catheters   WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW:   A catheter is a small tube used to give treatments and to take blood. The catheter is guided into place through a peripheral vein in your upper arm. Peripheral veins lead from your arms and legs to your heart. A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) is guided into a vein near the heart. A midline catheter is guided into a vein below the armpit.   DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:   Prevent catheter-associated infections:  The area around your catheter may get infected, or you may get an infection in your bloodstream. A catheter-associated infection is caused by bacteria (germs) getting into your bloodstream through your catheter. Infections from catheters can lead to severe illness. The following are ways you can help prevent an infection:  � Wash your hands:  Use soap or an alcohol-based hand rub to clean your hands. Clean your hands before and after you touch the catheter or the catheter site. Ask your healthcare provider for information on how to wash your hands. Remind anyone who cares for your catheter to wash their hands.     � Wear medical gloves:  Wear clean medical gloves when you touch your catheter or change bandages.     � Limit contact:  Do not touch or handle your catheter unless you need to care for it. Do not pull, push on, or move the catheter when you clean your skin or change the bandage.    � Clean your skin:  Clean the skin around your catheter every day and just before you change your bandage. Ask your healthcare provider what to use when you clean your skin.     � Check for infection:  Check your skin every day for signs of infection, such as pain, redness, swelling, and oozing. Contact your healthcare provider if you see these signs.    � Cover the area:  Keep a sterile bandage over the catheter site. Change the bandage as directed or when it is loose, wet, dirty, or falls off. Change your bandage in a 
place away from open windows, heating ducts, and fans. Be sure it is well-lit, clean, and free of dust. Clean the skin under the bandage with the solution your healthcare provider suggests. Let the area dry before you put on the new bandage.    � Keep the area dry:  Do not let your catheter or catheter site get wet. Wrap your arm with plastic and seal with medical tape before you bathe. Ask if you should take showers instead of baths.  Care for your PICC or midline catheter:  Your healthcare provider may want you to do the following to reduce your risk of infection or complications:  � Clean your catheter parts:  Clean the caps, hubs, and injection ports before you attach and after you remove tubing from your catheter. Open the package that contains the new alcohol pad. Put on new medical gloves. Use a new alcohol pad for each part you clean. Throw away used alcohol pads.    � Flush your catheter:  Your healthcare provider may give you syringes filled with saline (salt water) or heparin to flush your catheter. Heparin is a medicine that helps prevent blood clots from forming inside the catheter. Heparin can cause an allergic reaction and bleeding problems.     � Attach the syringe that contains the flushing solution to the end of the catheter tubing. Slowly push the fluid out of the syringe and into the catheter. Throw away the syringe. Clean the end of the catheter or cap with a new alcohol pad.    � Do not force the fluid. Force could damage the catheter, or release a blood clot from the end of the catheter. Straighten any kinks in the tubing. Contact your healthcare provider if it is still hard to push fluid into the catheter.    � Change the caps and medicine tubing:  You may need to use extra tubing to get medicine. Ask your healthcare provider how often to change the caps and the medicine tubing.     � Clamp the catheter:  You may need to clamp your catheter at certain times, such as when the tubing is being 
changed. The catheter is clamped to help prevent air from getting in.    � Loop extra tubing:  Loosely loop the tubing together. Secure it to your arm with medical tape. This will help prevent the PICC or midline catheter from being pulled out by accident.  Follow up with your healthcare provider as directed:  Write down your questions so you remember to ask them during your visits.   NSAIDs:  This medicine will help decrease pain and redness where the catheter enters your skin. You can buy NSAIDs without a prescription. NSAIDs can cause stomach bleeding or kidney problems if you do not take them correctly. Always read the medicine label and follow the directions before you use this medicine.  Warm compresses:  The area where the catheter was inserted may feel sore. A warm compress can help to decrease pain and swelling in your arm. Wet a small towel with warm water. Wring out the extra water. Wrap the cloth in plastic, and put it on the area. Use the compress 4 times a day, for 10 minutes each time. Prop your arm up on pillows when you are sitting or lying down. This will decrease swelling.   Contact your healthcare provider if:   � You have a fever.     � The catheter site is red, warm, painful, or oozing fluid.    � You see blood on your bandage and the amount is increasing.     � The veins in your neck or chest bulge.     � You cannot flush your catheter, or you feel pain when you flush your catheter.     � You see that the catheter is getting shorter or it falls out. Put pressure over the site with a clean towel before you contact your healthcare provider.    � You see a hole or a crack in your catheter. Clamp your catheter above the damage before you contact your healthcare provider.     � You have questions about how to care for your catheter.    � You run out of supplies to care for your skin or catheter.  Return to the emergency department if:   � You feel pain in your arm, neck, shoulder, or 
chest.    � The catheter site turns cold, changes color, or you cannot feel it.    � You cough up blood.    � You see blisters on the skin near the catheter site.  � 2017 Popdust. PROCEDURE PERFORMED:  Incision and drainage and debridement of distal  brachial artery pseudoaneurysm, distal brachial artery to brachial  artery bypass with ipsilateral right greater saphenous vein on-table  angiogram.    SURGEON:  Min Newell MD    ANESTHESIA:  General.    ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS:  400 mL.    COMPLICATIONS ENCOUNTERED:  None.    SPECIMEN SENT:  Wall of aneurysm, was sent for tissue culture.    INDICATIONS:  A 39-year-old male patient who presented to the emerRiver Valley Medical Center  department with hemorrhage from a laceration in the right antecubital  fossa which was arterial, brisk and required application of two  tourniquets by prehospital care providers.    DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE:  The patient was brought to the operating  room, placed in the supine position.  General anesthesia was induced.   He was prepped and draped in a standard fashion.  Preoperative time-out  was conducted.    Attention was turned onto the right upper extremity.  The two  tourniquets placed by prehospital care were removed and a pneumatic  tourniquet was placed and inflated to 250 mmHg.  Next, the brachial  artery proximal to the injury was exposed through a standard  longitudinal incision and it was dissected circumferentially and vessel  loop proximally and distally.  It was occluded with a vascular clamp 
and  pneumatic tourniquet was then released.  Attention was then turned to  the area distal to the injury where the brachial artery distal to the  aneurysm was exposed through a longitudinal incision, dissected  circumferentially.  This incision was then extended proximally to the  area of the pseudoaneurysm with proximal and distal control obtained.   The pseudoaneurysm was debrided identifying and ligating multiple  arterial and venous branches.  Once hemostasis was obtained, a length of  saphenous vein was harvested and preserved and on-table angiogram was  performed through the distal brachial artery to verify the vessel and  assessed the runoff, dominant runoff appeared to be through the ulnar  artery to the hand but the distal radial artery and pedal arch did not  opacify.  A brachial artery to brachial artery bypass was then performed  with the greater saphenous vein tunneling the saphenous vein medially  outside the area of obvious infection.  The proximal anastomosis was  sewn end-to-side with continuous 6-0 running suture.  The vein was then  flushed and it was sewn end-to-side to the distal anastomosis.  The  bypass graft was opened and good arterial flow was assessed including  strong Doppler signal at the ulnar artery, and the wrist and the hand  became warm and with good capillary refill.  The wounds were irrigated  with antibiotic saline solution and closed primarily with heavy 2-0  nylon suture.  The patient tolerated the procedure well, was taken  stable to postanesthesia care without complications. PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS  

L4-L5 degenerative disk disease with spondylolisthesis and neurogenic 
claudication.  



POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS 

L4-L5 degenerative disk disease with spondylolisthesis and neurogenic 
claudication.  



PROCEDURE PERFORMED 

L4-L5 laminectomy and L4-L5 posterolateral instrumented fusion.  



IV FLUIDS 

1700 mL. 



ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS 

150 mL.



IMPLANTS

6.5 mm x 45 mm Reline pedicle screws from NuVasive x 4, a 35 mm connecting priyanka 
and a 40 mm connecting priyanka also from NuVasive and locking caps x 4 from 
NuVasive.  



SPECIMENS

None.



DRAINS

None.



COMPLICATIONS

An incidental durotomy occurred, and will be described later in the procedure.  



INDICATIONS FOR SURGERY

Mr. Griffin an 80-year-old avid cyclist who presented to my clinic with complaint 
of worsening right greater than left pain, numbness and tingling in an L5 
distribution down bilateral lower extremities.  In addition to this, he noted 
decreased walking tolerance secondary to heaviness and tiredness in his legs.  
His physical examination was essentially unremarkable, but his MRI showed 
severe spinal stenosis at the L4-L5 level, and flexion and extension x-rays 
showed significantly dynamic spondylolisthesis at L4-L5.  Mr. Griffin had failed 
physical therapy, medications and activity modifications, and was therefore 
offered and elected to undergo L4-L5 laminectomy and fusion. 



Prior to surgery, I explained in detail to the patient the possible risks of 
surgery.  This includes the risk of bleeding, infection, damage to surrounding 
structures, persistent and/or worsening pain, nerve root injury, spinal fluid 
leak, meningitis, , blindness, sexual dysfunction, autonomic nervous 
system dysfunction as well as other unforeseen medical and surgical 
complications. An understanding that spinal surgery is more predictive in 
improving extremity discomfort than axial spine pain was stressed.  



DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE   

On the date of surgery, the patient was admitted to the preoperative hold area, 
and all questions were answered.  The operative site was identified and marked 
by myself.  The patient was brought in good condition to the operating room, 
and after succumbing to anesthesia, was placed in the prone position on a 
Grady table.  All bony protuberances and soft tissues were well padded in the 
standard fashion.  Preoperative antibiotics were administered according to the 
appropriate timing schedule.  Care was taken to maintain appropriate perfusion 
pressures during anesthesia.  At the conclusion of the procedure, sponge and 
needle count were correct x 2.  



Final time out was undertaken by members of the operating team to confirm 
correct patient, correct levels and correct surgery.  An incision was then made 
over the intended surgical levels, and sharp dissection was carried out down to 
the posterior elements.  Soft tissues were elevated off the posterior elements 
in a subperiosteal manner, and a lateral radiograph was obtained to confirm 
correct level.  At this point, a rongeur was used to remove the spinous process 
of L4. The lamina was thinned in the midline, and a Luna curette was used to 
undermine the superior insertion of the ligamentum flavum on the inferior 
surface of the L4 lamina.  The canal was entered, and a Carlton elevator was 
utilized to separate dura from surrounding soft tissue and bone prior to use of 
the Kerrison punch.  A 4-0 Kerrison rongeur was then used to perform midline 
decompression.  At the superior aspect of this decompression, we encountered a 
large arachnoid cyst. We packed this of with a surgical david in hopes that it 
would not become a full thickness dural tear.  Unfortunately, during the 
lateral recess decompressions, the arachnoid cyst gave way, and a significant 
amount of spinal fluid began leaking.  We therefore packed that off again, and 
placed the patient in 5 degrees of Trendelenburg.  We proceeded with bilateral 
lateral recess decompressions, taking care to thoroughly decompress the lateral 
recesses at that L4-L5 level, and also ensure that the foramina for the L5 and 
the L4 nerves were well decompressed. Once this was accomplished, we turned our 
attention to placement of pedicle screws.  Appropriate starting points for 
pedicle screws were identified at approximately the junction of the pars 
interarticularis, the midpoint of the transverse process and the lateral aspect 
of the superior articular process.  A high-speed yoel was used to decorticate, 
and then a Lenke-type probe was used to advance resistance through the isthmus 
of the pedicle and into the vertebral body.  A ball tip feeler was then used to 
palpate the pedicle superiorly, inferiorly, medial and laterally as well as 
distally to ensure absence of bony breaching.  Once this was confirmed, 6.5 mm 
x 45 mm screws were placed bilaterally at L4 and bilaterally at L5.  All screws 
had good purchase, and neurophysiologic monitoring was used to test the screws, 
all of which tested well above expected levels.  Lateral radiograph was 
obtained to confirm correct placement of all screws.  



At this point, 2 L of sterile saline were used to irrigate the wound, and we 
then decorticated the transverse processes of L4 and L5 bilaterally.  Bone that 
had been previously removed during the laminectomy portion of the procedure was 
run through a bone mill and then packed in the lateral recesses.  Surgical 
patties were then removed from the durotomy, and two pieces of DuraGen were 
placed in a elizabeth cross fashion over the durotomy and the arachnoid cyst.  The 
entire laminectomy defect was then sealed utilizing DuraSeal.  Once this was 
completed, no CSF leakage was noted.  



The wound was then closed in layers using interrupted sutures for the deep 
fascia, interrupted sutures for the subcutaneous tissue and then a running 
subcuticular skin stitch.  Sponge and needle counts were correct x 2.



POSTOPERATIVE CARE PLAN

We will keep Mr. Griffin flat overnight to give his durotomy an opportunity to 
heal.  We will begin gradually sitting him up midmorning tomorrow.  He will 
likely discharge home on  or  of this week, and will follow up 
in my clinic in two weeks time for wound check and examination.
